baseline_rows.pred_answer: Article 13 requires that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately. An appropriate type and degree of transparency must be ensured with a view to achieving compliance with the relevant obligations of both the provider and the deployer. The system must be accompanied by instructions for use in an appropriate digital format or otherwise, containing concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers, covering the provider's identity, the system's intended purpose, its capabilities and limitations, known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and the level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

Not automatically high-risk, but high-risk on two possible routes under Article 6. The first route under Article 6(1) applies if the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I that must undergo third-party conformity assessment; a clinical-trial patient-selection tool that qualifies as a medical device or in vitro diagnostic device under the legislation listed in Annex I and requires such assessment would satisfy this route. The second route under Article 6(2) applies if the system falls within a use case listed in Annex III; patient selection and recruitment for clinical trials is not listed there, and the employment and worker management category in Annex III covers recruitment and selection of natural persons in the employment context, not clinical-trial enrolment, so that category does not apply on its face. Where neither route is satisfied, the system is not high-risk, and the principal obligation that remains is the Article 50(1) transparency duty where the system interacts directly with natural persons. The deciding condition is therefore whether the system constitutes a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment.

The high-risk AI radiology system must technically allow for the automatic recording of events over its lifetime, with logging capabilities providing a level of traceability appropriate to the intended purpose, including events relevant to identifying risks and facilitating post-market monitoring (Article 12). The deploying hospital, as deployer, must keep those automatically generated logs for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law, in particular Union law on the protection of personal data, requires otherwise (Article 26(6)). The provider bears a parallel obligation to keep the same logs for at least six months under Article 19, and must separately retain the technical documentation, quality management system documentation, any notified body approvals, and the EU declaration of conformity for ten years after the system is placed on the market (Article 18).

No, the EU AI Act mandates no specific explainable-AI technique such as LIME or SHAP, and Article 13 instead requires only that high-risk AI systems be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret their output. Article 14 requires effective human oversight, and Article 15 requires appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. The Act is technique-agnostic, so the choice of any interpretability method is left to the provider.

The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems have no mandatory duties under the Act, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

Article 14 is the operative provision. A high-risk clinical decision-support system must be designed and developed so that the natural persons assigned to oversight can properly understand the system's capacities and limitations and duly monitor its operation, including by detecting anomalies and dysfunctions (Article 14(4)(a)); remain aware of the possible tendency to automatically rely or over-rely on the system's output, that is, automation bias (Article 14(4)(b)); correctly interpret the system's output, taking into account available interpretation tools and methods (Article 14(4)(c)); and decide, in any particular situation, not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output (Article 14(4)(d)). Article 26(2) places the corresponding deployer duty: the deployer must assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support. Article 13 requires the provider to supply instructions for use that describe those human oversight measures and the technical measures put in place to facilitate interpretation of the system's outputs, so that the deployer can implement oversight in practice.

A biometric patient identification system at hospital check-in is high-risk only where it qualifies as a remote biometric identification system under Annex III(1)(a), meaning it identifies natural persons without their active involvement by comparing biometric data against a reference database, and that classification is excluded where the system is used solely for biometric verification, that is, confirming that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Where the system operates as a one-to-one verification at check-in, with the patient actively presenting themselves for confirmation of their claimed identity, it falls within the Annex III(1)(a) exclusion and is not high-risk on that route. It may still be high-risk under Article 6(1) if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device or other product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I that is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Where neither route applies, the system is limited risk, and the deployer must inform patients of the operation of the system under Article 50(3) if it also performs biometric categorisation.

An AI safety component within a medical device of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III is high-risk under the EU AI Act. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where two cumulative conditions are met: the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Annex I lists Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and MDR class IIa, IIb, and III devices are all subject to third-party conformity assessment involving a notified body under that Regulation, satisfying both conditions. Consequently, the conformity assessment procedure for such a system is governed by Article 43(3), under which the provider follows the MDR's own conformity assessment procedure and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements of the EU AI Act form part of that assessment.

Melanoma-detection software of this kind is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device that must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. That classification follows Article 6(1), which sets two cumulative conditions: the system must be a safety component of, or itself constitute, a product covered by Annex I legislation, and that product must be subject to third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Where both conditions are met, the conformity assessment procedure is governed by Article 43(3), which requires the provider to follow the relevant sectoral procedure and treats the Chapter III Section 2 requirements as part of that assessment, with notified-body involvement where the sectoral legislation requires it.

For high-risk AI systems the applicable penalty ceiling is set by Article 99(4): administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the obligations on providers, deployers, importers and distributors (every obligation other than the Article 5 prohibitions, which carry the higher Article 99(3) ceiling of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 %). Under Article 99(6), for SMEs and start-ups each fine is capped at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

Non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices listed in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35,000,000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(3). For SMEs and start-ups, Article 99(6) provides that the applicable ceiling is the lower of the fixed amount and the percentage figure.

Annex III(3) lists four education and vocational training use cases that Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk: systems intended to determine access, admission or assignment of natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes, including where those outcomes are used to steer the learning process; systems intended to assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or be able to access within such institutions; and systems intended to monitor and detect prohibited behaviour of students during tests. A provider may rely on the Article 6(3) derogation and conclude that an Annex III(3) system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and where it performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the prior human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. A system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk regardless of those conditions. A provider relying on the derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market and must still register the system under Article 49(2).

The Regulation does not impose a general obligation to provide market surveillance authorities with remote access to documentation and datasets. The operative provision is Article 16(k), which requires a provider, upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, to demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system with the applicable requirements. Article 21 reinforces this by requiring providers to make available to competent authorities, on request, all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate that conformity. These are request-based, on-demand duties rather than a standing obligation to grant remote access. The Regulation does not specify that access must be remote, nor does it require providers to maintain a live or continuous connection to their documentation or datasets for surveillance purposes.

The EU AI Act does not itself confer jurisdiction on the Court of Justice of the European Union over Commission fine decisions against general-purpose AI model providers, nor does it specify what the Court may do with such a fine. Article 99 sets the administrative fine ceilings and the factors governing their imposition, but it addresses the conduct of market surveillance authorities and the Commission acting under the Act's enforcement framework, not the Court's supervisory role over those decisions. The question of judicial review jurisdiction and the Court's powers to cancel, reduce or uphold a fine falls under the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and the general principles of EU administrative law, which fall outside the scope of this Regulation.

The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.

No, historical provenance is irrelevant. Classification under Article 6(2) turns on the system's current intended purpose, not its prior use. Once the intended purpose no longer falls within any Annex III use case, the Annex III route to high-risk status no longer applies, and the system is not high-risk on that basis. The Article 6(1) route remains separately available if the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I legislation that requires third-party conformity assessment, but that depends on the new intended purpose, not the old one.

The Commission is empowered to amend Annex III, but only under the specific conditions Article 7 sets out. Article 7(1) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to update the list of high-risk use cases in Annex III by adding new areas or use cases, or by modifying existing ones, where both of two cumulative conditions are met: the AI system in question is intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III, or poses a risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights that is, having regard to its severity and probability of occurrence, equivalent to or greater than the harm posed by the use cases already listed, and the system poses a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons. Article 7(2) requires the Commission, when assessing whether those conditions are met, to take into account a set of criteria including the intended purpose of the system, the extent to which it has been used or is likely to be used, the nature and extent of the harm or adverse impact it could produce, the number of persons affected, the dependency of those persons on the outcome, the reversibility of the harm, the degree to which persons are in a position of vulnerability, the extent to which Union law already provides for effective measures to address the risk, and the potential for the harm to affect a particularly vulnerable group. The Commission is separately empowered under Article 6(6) to adopt delegated acts to amend the conditions in Article 6(3) under which an Annex III system may be treated as not high-risk, where there is concrete and reliable evidence of AI systems within Annex III's scope that do not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights.

Not automatically. Article 6(2) classifies an Annex III system as high-risk, but Article 6(3) provides a derogation: an Annex III system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and where it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or to perform a preparatory task. That derogation is unavailable where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case the system is always high-risk regardless of the other conditions. A provider relying on the Article 6(3) derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market and must still register the system under Article 49(2).

Article 50(1) imposes a provider obligation: AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must be designed so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person given the circumstances and context of use. That obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, but the exemption is reversed where those systems are available to the public to report a criminal offence. The information must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction, and must conform to applicable accessibility requirements, as Article 50(5) requires.

Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

Yes. Under Article 11(1), SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the technical documentation elements set out in Annex IV in a simplified manner, using a simplified form the Commission is required to establish for the needs of small and micro enterprises. Where an SME opts to use that form, the notified body performing the conformity assessment must accept it.

A deployer of a high-risk AI system must comply with four main obligations under the Regulation. Under Article 26, the deployer must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, monitor the system's operation and inform the provider where a risk or serious incident is identified, retain automatically generated logs, and inform affected workers where the system is deployed in the workplace. Under Article 27, deployers of Annex III systems, and deployers that are public authorities, must conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, covering the deployment process, affected persons, specific risks and human oversight measures, and must notify the market surveillance authority of the results. Under Article 13, the deployer is entitled to receive instructions for use that are sufficiently transparent to enable correct interpretation and appropriate use of the system's output, which is a provider design duty that directly conditions how the deployer can fulfil its own obligations. Under Article 86, any person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of a high-risk Annex III system's output, where that decision produces legal effects or similarly significant adverse effects on health, safety or fundamental rights, has the right to obtain from the deployer a clear and meaningful explanation of the AI system's role in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

Yes. Under Article 26(7), a deployer that is an employer must, before putting a high-risk AI system into service or using it at the workplace, inform the workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of that high-risk AI system. Under Article 26(7), that information must be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on the information of workers and their representatives.

The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

A hospital that fine-tunes an open-weight medical language model becomes a provider under Article 25(1) at the point it makes a substantial modification to the system, because Article 25(1) provides that a deployer or other third party that makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system assumes all provider obligations under the Regulation. Where the fine-tuning does not rise to a substantial modification but the hospital places its own name or trademark on the system, Article 25(1) equally triggers provider status at that moment. The question of whether the resulting system is high-risk, and therefore which full set of provider obligations attaches, turns on the classification analysis under Article 6, but the role-change itself occurs at whichever of those two events happens first.

As part of their supervisory role for an AI regulatory sandbox, market surveillance authorities must verify compliance with Article 57, which requires each Member State to establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox providing a controlled environment for developing, training, testing and validating innovative AI systems for a limited time before they are placed on the market or put into service.

Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

Under Article 50(4), a deployer that uses an AI system to generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. Under Article 50(4), that disclosure duty does not apply in two cases: first, where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; and second, where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.

An AI system used to dispatch and triage emergency-room patients is high-risk. Annex III(5)(d) expressly lists AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls, to dispatch or establish priority in the dispatching of emergency first response services including medical aid, and emergency healthcare patient triage systems, and Article 6(2) classifies every system listed in Annex III as high-risk.

Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system.

The AI system is high-risk under the EU AI Act, not "medium-risk." The Act uses only the binary classification of high-risk or not high-risk; it does not adopt the sectoral risk tiers of medical device legislation, and the term "medium-risk" has no meaning within it. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk where two cumulative conditions are met: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Medical devices are listed in Annex I, and the scenario states that the device undergoes third-party conformity assessment, so both conditions are satisfied and the AI system is high-risk by operation of Article 6(1), regardless of how the device is classified under medical device legislation. For conformity assessment, Article 43(3) provides that the provider follows the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under the applicable Annex I legislation, that the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that assessment, and that the notified body already notified under the sectoral legislation is entitled to control conformity with those requirements, yielding a single integrated procedure rather than two separate ones.

No, such a system is outside the Regulation's scope. Article 2(6) excludes AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, meaning no obligation under the Regulation applies to them. The exclusion is conditional on that sole purpose: a system that is also placed on the market, put into service for operational use, or whose output is used in the Union outside a pure research context falls back within the scope defined by Article 2(1).

Defining the "best" restaurant in Rome is quite subjective, as it depends on your personal preferences, budget, and the type of cuisine you're looking for! Rome boasts an incredible variety of dining options, from traditional trattorias serving classic Roman dishes to Michelin-starred establishments.

Not automatically. Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk only those AI systems that fall within a specific use case listed in Annex III, not every system that operates in one of Annex III's eight subject-matter areas. A system that operates in, for example, the law enforcement area but does not correspond to any of the enumerated use cases within that area is not classified as high-risk under Article 6(2). Such a system may still be high-risk under Article 6(1) if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, but absent that route it falls outside the high-risk classification.

AI medical device software that is itself a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Medical Device Regulation or the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (both listed in Annex I, points 11 and 12) is high-risk under Article 6(1), provided that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. For such a system, Article 43(3) prescribes a single integrated route: the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required by the Medical Device Regulation or the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements of the EU AI Act form part of that same assessment, conducted by the notified body already notified under the sectoral legislation. A new conformity assessment procedure is required whenever the system undergoes a substantial modification, as Article 43(4) provides. The timeline question, including the application dates under the Medical Device Regulation or the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, falls outside the scope of this Regulation and must be addressed under those instruments.

A controlled framework set up by a competent authority which offers providers or prospective providers of AI systems the possibility to develop, train, validate and test, where appropriate in real-world conditions, an innovative AI system, pursuant to a sandbox plan for a limited time under regulatory supervision.

Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

The transparency obligations that apply to a content-moderation AI system operated by a Very Large Online Platform depend on the role of the party and the nature of the system's outputs. Where the platform is the provider of an AI system designed to interact directly with natural persons, Article 50(1) requires the system to be designed so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system. Where the system generates synthetic content, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated. Where the platform is the deployer, Article 50(4) imposes two distinct duties. First, where the system generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake, the deployer must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated; this duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute a criminal offence, and where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional work the disclosure obligation is limited to an appropriate disclosure that does not hamper enjoyment of the work. Second, where the system generates or manipulates text published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, the deployer must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated; this duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, or where the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication. If the content-moderation AI is itself a high-risk system, Article 13 additionally requires it to be designed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable the deployer to interpret its output and use it appropriately, accompanied by instructions for use that are concise, complete, correct and clear.

Systemic risk applies to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

Article 1 states that the purpose of the Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation. To achieve that purpose, Article 1 lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems; prohibitions of certain AI practices; specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models; rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement; and measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups.

Not high-risk under the described intended purpose. An ambient scribe that only transcribes doctor-patient consultations and performs no diagnosis or decision-making does not fall within either route under Article 6: it is not described as a safety component of, or itself a product covered by, Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and transcription alone does not correspond to any of the Annex III use cases. Even if a marginal Annex III argument were raised, the system would qualify for the Article 6(3) derogation because pure transcription is a narrow procedural task that does not materially influence the outcome of decision making and does not constitute profiling of natural persons. The system therefore sits at the minimal risk tier, carrying no Chapter III Section 2 obligations, though the provider should document the Article 6(3) self-assessment before placing the system on the market and register under Article 49(2) if relying on that derogation.

The question is broad, so the answer maps the Regulation's structure rather than a specific system's obligations. The starting point is Article 1, which establishes that the Regulation lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union, together with prohibitions of certain AI practices, requirements for high-risk AI systems, transparency rules, and rules for general-purpose AI models. A company must first determine which category its AI systems fall into, because the obligations differ by tier. Systems engaging in practices listed as prohibited under Article 5 must not be placed on the market or used at all. High-risk systems, classified under Article 6, must satisfy the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, which Article 8 frames as compliance with those requirements taking into account the intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art, with the risk management system under Article 9 as the organising mechanism. Providers of general-purpose AI models must comply with the obligations in Chapter V, and where the Commission identifies systemic risk it may, under Article 93, require the provider to take mitigation measures, restrict availability, or withdraw the model. Transitional timing matters: Article 111 provides that providers of general-purpose AI models already on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027, and operators of high-risk systems intended for use by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030.

Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service, or using an AI system for emotion recognition in the workplace and in educational institutions, with a narrow carve-out for systems used for medical or safety reasons. Outside those two settings, emotion recognition is not prohibited by Article 5(1)(f), though it may fall within the high-risk use case listed in Annex III(1)(c) and attract the full Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Regardless of risk tier, a deployer operating an emotion recognition system must inform the natural persons exposed to it of the system's operation, under Article 50(3), and that information must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first exposure. The Article 50(3) duty does not apply where the system is permitted by law to detect, prevent, or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties.

An AI system that is a safety component of a CE-marked medical device is high-risk under Article 6(1), provided both cumulative conditions are met: the system is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Where those conditions are satisfied, Article 43(3) applies: the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure prescribed by the applicable Annex I sectoral legislation, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements of the EU AI Act form part of that assessment rather than triggering a separate AI-specific conformity assessment procedure.

An oncology treatment recommendation tool falls within Annex III(5)(b), which covers AI systems intended to be used in the management and operation of critical infrastructure, and more directly within Annex III(5)(a) as a system used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public services including healthcare, making it high-risk under Article 6(2) where those conditions are met; where the deployer is a private entity outside the public-authority limb, the provider must still assess whether the Article 6(3) derogation applies, documenting that assessment before placing the system on the market and registering under Article 49(2) if relying on it. As a high-risk system, the provider must satisfy the full Chapter III Section 2 obligation chain: a risk management system established, implemented, documented and maintained across the entire lifecycle identifying and analysing known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights and adopting targeted mitigation measures (Article 9); data governance ensuring training, validation and test datasets are relevant, representative, free of errors and complete, with bias examination and, where strictly necessary, controlled processing of special-category personal data (Article 10); technical documentation drawn up before market placement per Annex IV, including a post-market monitoring plan (Article 11); automatic logging of events throughout operation kept for at least six months (Article 12 and Article 19); transparency to deployers through instructions for use covering the system's capabilities, limitations, accuracy metrics and human-oversight measures (Article 13); accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity maintained consistently throughout the lifecycle with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use (Article 15); and a quality management system covering regulatory-compliance strategy, design verification, test procedures, post-market monitoring and incident-reporting workflows (Article 17). Before placing the system on the market the provider must have it undergo conformity assessment (Article 43), draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), affix the CE marking (Article 48), and register in the EU database (Article 49), as consolidated in the provider obligations listed in Article 16. Post-placement, the provider must operate a post-market monitoring system that actively and systematically collects and analyses data on the system's performance throughout its lifetime and feeds findings back into the risk management system (Article 72), and must report any serious incident to the relevant market surveillance authority (Article 73). A provider established outside the Union must appoint, by written mandate, an authorised representative established in the Union before placing the system on the market, empowered to verify compliance documentation, keep it available for ten years, supply it to competent authorities on reasoned request, and cooperate with market surveillance authorities (Article 22). If the tool is built on or constitutes a general-purpose AI model, that model regime runs parallel to the high-risk tier: the model provider must maintain technical documentation per Annex XI, supply downstream-provider information per Annex XII, implement a copyright policy and publish a training-data summary (Article 53), and where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations the additional systemic-risk obligations of Article 55 apply on top.
