Non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices listed in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35,000,000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(3). For SMEs and start-ups, Article 99(6) provides that the applicable ceiling is the lower of the fixed amount and the percentage figure, rather than the higher.

Annex III(3) lists four education and vocational training use cases that Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk: systems intended to determine access, admission, or assignment of natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes, including where those outcomes are used to steer the learning process; systems intended to assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or be able to access; and systems intended to monitor and detect prohibited behaviour of students during tests. A provider may rely on the Article 6(3) derogation and conclude a system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing a prior human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, but a system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk regardless of those conditions. A provider relying on that derogation must document the self-assessment before placing the system on the market and must still register the system under Article 49(2).

The Regulation does not impose a general obligation to provide market surveillance authorities with remote access to documentation and datasets. The operative provision is Article 16(k), which requires a provider, upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, to demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system with the applicable requirements. Article 21 reinforces this by requiring providers to make available to competent authorities, on request, all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate that conformity. These are request-based, on-demand obligations rather than a standing remote-access entitlement. The Regulation does not specify that access must be provided remotely, nor does it require providers to maintain a live or continuous connection to their documentation or datasets for supervisory purposes.

The EU AI Act does not itself confer jurisdiction on the Court of Justice of the European Union over Commission fine decisions against general-purpose AI model providers, nor does it specify what the Court may do with such a fine. Article 99 sets the administrative fine ceilings, up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover for breaches of the obligations listed in Article 99(4), and up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information under Article 99(5), but Article 99 addresses the Commission's power to impose fines rather than judicial review of those decisions. The question of the Court's jurisdiction and its powers to annul, reduce or uphold a Commission fine falls under the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and the general principles of EU administrative law, which are outside the scope of this Regulation.

The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.

No, historical provenance is irrelevant. Classification under Article 6(2) turns on the system's current intended purpose, not its prior use. Once the intended purpose no longer falls within any Annex III use case, the Annex III route to high-risk classification no longer applies, and the system is not high-risk on that basis. The Article 6(1) route remains separately available if the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I legislation that requires third-party conformity assessment, but that depends on the new intended purpose, not the old one.

The Commission is empowered to amend Annex III, but only under the specific conditions Article 7 sets out. Article 7(1) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to update the list of high-risk use cases in Annex III where both of two cumulative conditions are met: the AI system in question is intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III, and it poses a risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights that is, having regard to its severity and probability of occurrence, equivalent to or greater than the risk of harm posed by the high-risk systems already listed there. Article 7(2) requires the Commission, when assessing whether those conditions are met, to take into account a set of criteria including the intended purpose, the extent to which the system has been used or is likely to be used, the nature and amount of data processed, the extent to which the system acts autonomously, the extent to which persons affected have the ability to opt out, the extent to which potential victims are in a vulnerable position, the extent to which the outcome is easily reversible, the magnitude and likelihood of a benefit to natural persons, and the number of persons affected. The Commission may also, by delegated act under Article 7(1), remove a use case from Annex III where it no longer meets those conditions. Separately, Article 6(6) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts to amend the conditions in Article 6(3) under which an Annex III system is treated as not high-risk, where there is concrete and reliable evidence of AI systems within the scope of Annex III that do not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights.

Not automatically. Article 6(2) classifies an Annex III system as high-risk, but Article 6(3) provides a derogation: an Annex III system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and where it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or to perform a preparatory task. That derogation is unavailable where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case the system is always high-risk regardless of the other conditions. A provider relying on the Article 6(3) derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market and must still register the system under Article 49(2).

Article 50(1) imposes a provider obligation: AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must be designed so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person given the circumstances and context of use. That obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, but the exception is reversed where those systems are available to the public to report a criminal offence. Where a system interacting with natural persons also operates as an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system, Article 50(3) imposes a separate deployer obligation: the deployer must inform the natural persons exposed to the system of its operation and process personal data in accordance with applicable Union data-protection law; that deployer obligation does not apply to systems permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards. The information required under Article 50(1) and Article 50(3) must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform to applicable accessibility requirements.

Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

Yes. Under Article 11(1), SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the technical documentation elements set out in Annex IV in a simplified manner, using a simplified form the Commission is required to establish for the needs of small and micro enterprises. Where an SME opts to use that form, the notified body performing the conformity assessment must accept it.

A deployer of a high-risk AI system must comply with four main obligations under the Regulation. Under Article 26, the deployer must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, monitor the operation of the system and inform the provider where a risk or serious incident is identified, retain automatically generated logs, and inform affected workers where the system is used in the workplace. Under Article 27, deployers of Annex III systems, and deployers that are public authorities, must conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, covering the deployment process, affected persons, specific risks and human oversight measures, and must notify the market surveillance authority of the results. Under Article 13, the deployer is entitled to receive a system designed and accompanied by instructions for use that are sufficiently transparent to enable the deployer to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately. Under Article 86, where the deployer takes a decision on the basis of the output of an Annex III high-risk system (excluding Annex III point 2 critical infrastructure systems) that produces legal effects or similarly significantly adverse effects on a person's health, safety or fundamental rights, that person has the right to obtain from the deployer a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

Yes. Under Article 26(7), a deployer that is an employer must, before putting a high-risk AI system into service or using it at the workplace, inform the workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of that high-risk AI system. Under Article 26(7), that information must be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on the information of workers and their representatives.

The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

A hospital that fine-tunes an open-weight medical language model becomes a provider under Article 25(1) at the point it makes a substantial modification to the system, because Article 25(1) provides that a deployer or other third party that makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system assumes all provider obligations under the Regulation. Where the fine-tuning does not rise to a substantial modification but the hospital places its own name or trademark on the system, Article 25(1) equally triggers provider status at that moment. The question of whether the resulting system is high-risk, and therefore which full set of provider obligations attaches, turns on the classification analysis under Article 6, but the role-change itself occurs at whichever of those two events happens first.

As part of their supervisory role for an AI regulatory sandbox, market surveillance authorities must verify compliance with Article 57, which requires each Member State to establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox providing a controlled environment for developing, training, testing and validating innovative AI systems for a limited time before they are placed on the market or put into service.

Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

Under Article 50(4), a deployer that uses an AI system to generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. Under Article 50(4), that disclosure duty does not apply in two cases: first, where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; and second, where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.

An AI system used to dispatch and triage emergency-room patients is high-risk. Annex III(5)(d), read with Article 6(2), expressly lists AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls, to dispatch or establish priority in the dispatching of emergency first response services including medical aid, and emergency healthcare patient triage systems as high-risk use cases.

Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system.

The AI system is high-risk under the EU AI Act, not "medium-risk." The Act uses only the binary classification of high-risk or not high-risk; it does not adopt the sectoral risk tiers of medical device legislation, and the term "medium-risk" has no meaning within it. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk where two cumulative conditions are met: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Medical devices are listed in Annex I, and the scenario states that the device undergoes third-party conformity assessment, so both conditions are satisfied and the AI system is high-risk by operation of Article 6(1) alone, regardless of how the device is classified under medical device legislation. For conformity assessment, Article 43(3) provides that the provider follows the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under the applicable Annex I legislation, that the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that assessment, and that notified bodies already notified under that legislation are entitled to control conformity with those requirements, yielding a single integrated procedure rather than two separate ones.

No, such a system is outside the scope of the Regulation. Article 2(6) expressly excludes AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, so a biomedical research system that is not placed on the market falls entirely outside the Regulation's obligations. The exclusion is conditional on two cumulative requirements: the system must be specifically developed for that purpose, and it must not be placed on the market or put into service for any other use.

One of the most highly praised restaurants in Rome is Roscioli, a gourmet deli‑restaurant near Campo de’ Fiori that blends classic Roman dishes (like carbonara and cacio e pepe) with an extensive wine list and top‑quality ingredients. Reservations are recommended, especially for dinner.

Not automatically. Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk only where it falls within one of the specific use cases listed in Annex III, not merely because it operates in one of Annex III's eight subject-matter areas. A system that operates in, for example, the law enforcement area but does not correspond to any of the enumerated use cases within that area is not classified as high-risk under Article 6(2).

AI medical device software that is itself a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Medical Device Regulation or the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (both listed in Annex I, points 11 and 12) is high-risk under Article 6(1), provided that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under those instruments. For such a system, Article 43(3) directs the provider to follow the conformity assessment procedure required by the applicable sectoral legislation, meaning the notified-body route under the Medical Device Regulation or the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements of the EU AI Act form part of that single assessment. The notified body already notified under those sectoral instruments is entitled to control conformity with the EU AI Act requirements within the same procedure, provided its compliance with the relevant competence conditions has been assessed in the context of that notification. Where the sectoral legislation permits the product manufacturer to opt out of third-party assessment because all relevant harmonised standards have been applied, that opt-out is available under Article 43(3) only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Chapter III Section 2 requirements of the EU AI Act. A substantial modification to the system triggers a new conformity assessment procedure under Article 43(4).

A controlled framework set up by a competent authority which offers providers or prospective providers of AI systems the possibility to develop, train, validate and test, where appropriate in real-world conditions, an innovative AI system, pursuant to a sandbox plan for a limited time under regulatory supervision.

Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

The transparency obligations that apply to a content-moderation AI system operated by a Very Large Online Platform depend on the role of the party and the function of the system. The provider of the system must ensure, under Article 50(1), that it is designed so that natural persons interacting with it are informed they are interacting with an AI system. Where the system generates synthetic content, the provider must also mark those outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated, as required by Article 50(2). The deployer carries separate duties under Article 50(3) and Article 50(4). Article 50(3) requires the deployer to inform natural persons who are exposed to an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system. Article 50(4) imposes two distinct obligations: first, where the system generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake, the deployer must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, unless the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute a criminal offence, or the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional work, in which case disclosure is limited to what does not hamper enjoyment of the work; second, where the system generates or manipulates text published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, the deployer must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated, unless the use is authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes or the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for its publication. Where the content-moderation system is classified as high-risk under Article 6, Article 13 additionally requires it to be designed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable the deployer to interpret its output and use it appropriately, accompanied by instructions for use that are concise, complete, correct and clear.

Systemic risk applies to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

Article 1 states that the purpose of the Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation. To that end, Article 1 lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems; prohibitions of certain AI practices; specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models; rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement; and measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups.

Not high-risk under the described intended purpose. An ambient scribe that only transcribes doctor-patient consultations and performs no diagnosis or decision-making does not fall within any Annex III use case, and a pure transcription function is not a safety component of a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation, so neither route under Article 6(1) nor Article 6(2) is engaged. The system sits at the limited risk tier, and because it interacts directly with natural persons it carries the Article 50 transparency duty requiring the provider to design it so that those natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system.

The question is broad, so the answer maps the Regulation's structure rather than a specific system's obligations. The starting point is Article 1, which establishes that the Regulation lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union, together with prohibitions of certain AI practices, requirements for high-risk AI systems, transparency rules, and rules for general-purpose AI models. A company must first determine which category its AI systems fall into, because the obligations differ by tier. Systems engaging in practices listed as prohibited are barred from the market entirely. High-risk systems, classified under Article 6, must satisfy the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, which Article 8 frames by reference to the system's intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art, with the risk management system under Article 9 taken into account throughout. Where a company develops or places on the market a general-purpose AI model, the obligations in Chapter V apply, and Article 111 sets transitional deadlines, including that providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027, and that operators of high-risk systems intended for use by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030. The precise obligations for any given system depend on its classification, its intended purpose, and the role the company occupies, none of which the question specifies.

Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service, or using an AI system for emotion recognition in the workplace and in educational institutions, with a narrow carve-out where the system is used for medical or safety reasons. Outside those two settings, emotion recognition is not prohibited by Article 5(1)(f), though it may attract other obligations depending on how it is deployed. Where a deployer operates an emotion recognition system in any context, Article 50(3) requires that deployer to inform the natural persons exposed to the system of its operation. That information must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first exposure, as Article 50(5) requires.

An AI system that is a safety component of a CE-marked medical device is high-risk under Article 6(1), provided both cumulative conditions are met: the system is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Where those conditions are satisfied, Article 43(3) governs the conformity assessment route: the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure prescribed by the applicable Annex I sectoral legislation, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements of the EU AI Act form part of that assessment rather than triggering a separate AI-specific procedure.

An oncology treatment recommendation tool falls within Annex III(5)(b), which covers AI systems intended to be used in the management and operation of critical infrastructure, and more directly within Annex III(5)(a) as a system used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public services including healthcare, making it high-risk under Article 6(2) where those conditions are met; where the deployer is a private entity outside the public-authority limb, the provider must still assess whether the Article 6(3) derogation applies, documenting that assessment before placing the system on the market and registering under Article 49(2) if relying on it. As a high-risk system, the provider must satisfy the full Chapter III Section 2 obligation chain: a risk management system established, implemented, documented and maintained across the entire lifecycle identifying and analysing known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights and adopting targeted mitigation measures (Article 9); data governance ensuring training, validation and test datasets are relevant, representative, free of errors and complete, with bias examination and, where strictly necessary, controlled processing of special categories of personal data (Article 10); technical documentation drawn up before market placement and kept updated per Annex IV (Article 11); automatic logging of events throughout operation (Article 12); transparency to deployers through instructions for use covering the system's capabilities, limitations, accuracy metrics and human oversight measures (Article 13); human oversight measures enabling assigned persons to understand the system, detect automation bias, correctly interpret outputs and override or disregard them (Article 14); and appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity maintained throughout the lifecycle, with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use (Article 15). The provider must also operate a quality management system covering regulatory compliance strategy, design verification, test procedures, post-market monitoring and incident reporting workflows (Article 17); keep technical documentation, quality management system documentation and the EU declaration of conformity for ten years after market placement, and automatically generated logs for at least six months (Articles 18 and 19); undergo conformity assessment before placing the system on the market (Article 43); draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47); affix the CE marking (Article 48); and register in the EU database (Article 49), as consolidated in Article 16. Post-market monitoring must actively and systematically collect and analyse data on the system's performance throughout its lifetime, feeding results back into the iterative risk management system (Article 72), and serious incidents must be reported to the relevant market surveillance authority (Article 73). A provider established outside the Union must appoint, by written mandate, an authorised representative established in the Union before placing the system on the market, empowered to verify compliance, keep documentation available for ten years and cooperate with market surveillance authorities (Article 22). None of the Article 5(1) prohibited practices are engaged by a clinical guideline recommendation function on its own facts, provided the system does not deploy subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm (Article 5(1)(a)) or exploit patient vulnerabilities in a manner that distorts behaviour (Article 5(1)(b)); those prohibitions remain relevant as design constraints the provider must respect throughout development.

For a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, the provider must submit the information specified in Annex VIII Section A to the EU database established under Article 71, before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, as required by Article 49(1). That information comprises: the name, address and contact details of the provider; the name, address and contact details of any person submitting information on the provider's behalf; the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative where applicable; the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system and its operating logic; the status of the AI system on the market or in service; the type, number and expiry date of any certificate issued by a notified body and the name or identification number of that body; a scanned copy of that certificate where applicable; the Member States in which the system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47; electronic instructions for use; and an optional URL for additional information. Where the system falls within the law enforcement, migration, asylum or border control use cases listed in Annex III points 1, 6 and 7, Article 49(4) restricts registration to a secure non-public section of the EU database and limits the submitted information to Annex VIII Section A points 1 to 10 (excluding points 6, 8 and 9), omitting the certificate copy, the declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use.

Not prohibited and not high-risk. Annex III(1)(a) expressly excludes from the high-risk biometrics category AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. None of the Article 5(1) prohibited practices covers biometric verification of this kind. The system therefore falls outside both the prohibited tier and the Annex III high-risk classification, leaving it at limited risk subject to the Article 50 transparency obligations where it interacts directly with natural persons.

The answer depends on which procedure applies, but in neither case is immediate recall automatic. Where the MSA finds that a system the provider classified as non-high-risk under Article 6(3) is in fact high-risk, Article 80(2) governs: the authority requires the provider to take all necessary actions to bring the system into compliance with the Regulation's requirements and to take appropriate corrective action within a period the MSA may prescribe. Where the MSA has sufficient reason to consider that the system presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, Article 79(2) applies: after carrying out an evaluation, the authority requires the relevant operator to bring the system into compliance, withdraw it from the market, or recall it within a period the MSA prescribes, and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period provided for in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. Separately, under Article 20(1), a provider that itself considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk system it has placed on the market is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, which may include withdrawal, disabling or recall, and must inform distributors, deployers, authorised representatives and importers accordingly. The gravity of the situation therefore does influence the outcome: the MSA sets the corrective-action period proportionate to the risk, but the outer limit of 15 working days under Article 79(2) applies where a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights is found, whereas Article 80(2) leaves the period entirely to the MSA's prescription where the sole finding is misclassification without an identified risk of that kind.

No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

The question is conversational rather than a specific regulatory question about the EU AI Act, so a focused answer is not possible here. Please ask a specific question about a provision, obligation, system classification, role, or penalty under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and a precise answer will follow.

The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

Minimal risk. A consumer wellness chatbot that gives general lifestyle tips and makes no medical claims is not a safety component of a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation, and it does not fall within any of the Annex III use cases, so neither route under Article 6 classifies it as high-risk. Where the chatbot interacts directly with natural persons, Article 50 requires the provider to design it so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system.

Before placing a high-risk medical diagnostic system on the market, the provider must ensure it satisfies all the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and bears the provider's identifying details, as required by the overarching provider duty in Article 16. The system must meet the substantive design requirements of Article 8, supported by a documented, iterative risk-management system running across its lifecycle under Article 9, and data-governance practices ensuring the training, validation and test datasets are relevant, representative, complete and examined for bias under Article 10. The provider must draw up the technical documentation before placing the system on the market, demonstrating conformity and containing the content specified in Annex IV, as required by Article 11.

Testing data is defined in Article 3(32) as data used to provide an independent evaluation of the AI system, in order to confirm its expected performance before it is placed on the market or put into service. It must be kept separate from the training and validation data so that this evaluation is genuinely independent. If testing data leaks into the training process, the system is in effect assessed on data it has already seen, which inflates its apparent performance and defeats the purpose of the independent check that Article 10 requires for the datasets of a high-risk AI system.

Article 14 governs human oversight measures for high-risk AI systems, requiring that such systems be designed and developed in a way that allows assigned natural persons to understand the system's capacities and limitations, stay aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the output, decide not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output, and intervene or stop it. Article 26(2) places on the deployer the duty to assign that oversight to competent natural persons.

An AI system intended to be used by public authorities, or on behalf of public authorities, to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, is classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) read with Annex III(5)(a). The public-authority limb is load-bearing: a private system performing the same eligibility evaluation is not within Annex III(5)(a) and does not reach high-risk classification on that basis. The Article 6(3) derogation may remove the high-risk classification where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing a prior human assessment, or performs a preparatory task; however, a system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk and cannot rely on that derogation. The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems have no mandatory duties under the Act, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

Under the EU AI Act, the transparency obligations for a content-moderation AI on a Very Large Online Platform depend on the actor's role and the system's function. Where the content-moderation system interacts directly with natural persons, the provider must design it so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, as required by Article 50(1). Where the system generates synthetic audio, image, video or text outputs, the provider must mark those outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated, under Article 50(2). On the deployer side, Article 50(4) requires the deployer to disclose that image, audio or video content constituting a deepfake has been artificially generated or manipulated. Where the system generates or manipulates text published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, the deployer must also disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated; this duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, or where the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for its publication. The Digital Services Regulation, which governs Very Large Online Platforms' algorithmic transparency obligations as such, falls outside the scope of this Regulation.

Article 10 is the operative provision. Training, validation and testing datasets must be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, and must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of that purpose, with appropriate statistical properties as regards the persons or groups of persons on whom the system is intended to be used. The data governance practices required by Article 10(2) cover provenance, collection and selection methods, labelling procedures, data cleaning methodologies, and examination for possible biases likely to affect health and safety or to lead to discrimination. Where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, Article 10(5) permits the provider to process special categories of personal data, such as health data, subject to that necessity condition. The technical documentation required by Article 11, with content specified in Annex IV, must include datasheets describing the training methodologies and techniques, a general description of the training datasets, information about their provenance, scope and main characteristics, how the data was obtained and selected, labelling procedures, and data cleaning methodologies. A presumption of conformity with the Article 10(4) data governance requirements is available under Article 42(1) where the system has been trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used.
